en: Now begins the fourth chapter:
Here, the virtuous do not need to be entreated, for they proceed of their own accord; yet others cannot be compelled, for they suffer from an incurable aversion rooted in the bile of envy. (1)
I suspect that Indra, now bearing the happiness of his own kingdom without any apprehension, will somehow experience agitation toward those established in intense austerity;

for even in heaven, these men are indifferent to it, their delusion having vanished through the discernment of the meaning of Vedānta, which is made clear by the mere exposition composed by Vācaspatimiśra. (2)
START BsVBh_4,1.1.1:
Repetition [is required] because of the teaching that it is not [to be done] only once.

Since the attainment of the fruit is preceded by the performance of the means, he states the sequence of the two subjects of inquiry in accordance with the sequence of their objects—namely, in the third chapter.

Since the fruit characterized by liberation is entirely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*), the acts of seeing, hearing, reflecting, and meditating (*darśana-śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) enjoined for its sake have unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*); therefore, they must be performed according to their injunctions, but they should not be repeated beyond that, as there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such repetition.

However, regarding cases where the instruction is given only once, such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) and so forth, it might be argued that the performance should occur only once, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings. To this, the following is said in reply:

Although liberation has not been previously observed [in this world], nevertheless, because its nature—consisting in the Self’s abiding in its own true form through the eradication of ignorance along with its latent impressions—is established by scripture;

and because the eradication of ignorance by the arising of knowledge is logically established, just as the delusion of a snake is eradicated by the direct perception of the reality of the rope since ignorance is opposed to the arising of knowledge; and because, through positive and negative concomitance, it is established that the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration alone [leads to this].

Since the direct experience in the form of "I am the single conscious self entirely free from all suffering" is established in the world as having the fruit of directly realizing its own object, and since this experience is also inferred to have the means of practice such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth as its cause, hearing and the other practices have a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Moreover, when a visible purpose exists, it is not logical to assume an invisible purpose.
Furthermore, these [meditations] do not, by themselves, lead to such an experience characterized by direct realization through honor, long duration, and continuity.
Nor can a cognition that lacks direct realization here be capable of destroying ignorance which possesses direct realization.

Indeed, for one whose sense organ has been impaired by bile, the direct perception of bitterness in molasses cannot be removed even by a thousand logical arguments without the direct perception of its sweetness. Even if such a person considers the words of others who possess that knowledge or reflects upon thousands of arguments, he will only spit it out and discard the molasses. Thus, since meditation (*dhyāna*) and worship (*upāsana*) are observed in the world to have perceptible results and to consist of repeated mental activity, it is established that repetition is indeed required. //1//

And because of the indicative mark (liṅga). Having stated the meaning of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), he raises an objection regarding its having the attributeless Brahman as its object: "In this regard, it is said: 'Let it be so indeed... etc.
For the repetition of the mental state (*pratyaya*) is purposeful when the experience (*anubhava*) is something to be accomplished, but not when it is not.
Indeed, the experience of Brahman—the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—is not distinct from Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure.
And since the nature of the eternal Brahman is itself eternal, what need is there here for the repetition of the mental state?
This is what was stated: "having become one's very self" (*ātmabhūta*).
The opponent raises an objection: "upon hearing it once.

The intended meaning is this: the realization of Brahman as one's own self does not sever ignorance, because there is no contradiction [between them], as that [ignorance] continues to persist along with it.

Alternatively, if there were a contradiction [between the innate knowledge and ignorance], then because that [innate knowledge] is eternal, ignorance would not arise; how much less could it persist along with it?
Therefore, for its cessation, an adventitious direct realization of it must be sought.
And thus, the persistence of the cognitive condition is purposeful.
The objector objects by means of all the previous arguments, stating: "Even upon repetition [it does not produce direct realization].

Indeed, the cognition of the meaning of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sentence, even if repeated a hundred times, does not generate a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding its own object.
For even when such a cognition has arisen, it is merely intuitive (*prātibha*), because its deviation from reality has been observed.
The realization of the identity with Brahman (*brahmātmatva-pratīti*) is the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman as the Self.
Again, he raises an objection: "Not merely the sentence [is sufficient].
The objector refutes this: "Even so, repetition would be purposeless."

If a statement, depending upon reasoning, is capable of producing direct realization, then in that case there is no need for repetition; for once it has been applied along with its supporting arguments, it accomplishes what is to be done as long as it must be done. He raises a further objection: "But it might be argued..."
Reasoning and scriptural testimony do not have direct realization as their fruit, because that fruit belongs exclusively to the means of valid cognition that is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Those two, however, while apprehending an object beyond the senses, settle upon the mere universal (*sāmānya*) and do not directly realize the particular (*viśeṣa*); therefore, repeated practice is cultivated for the sake of the direct realization of that particular.

For when that practice is pursued with reverence, over a long period, and without interruption, it becomes a firm ground capable of bringing about the direct realization of the particular, just as the mental cultivation of a passionate woman leads to such a realization for a man of lustful nature.
The objector says: No;
[it occurs] even repeatedly.
Indeed, this direct realization (sākṣātkāra) must either have its source in scripture and reasoning, or have its source in mere cultivation (bhāvanā).

To begin with, scripture and reasoning—which have as their fruit a cognition that is a semblance of the imperceptible—are not capable of producing the fruit of direct perception, which is characterized by immediate realization.
Indeed, a banyan sprout does not arise from the seed of a *kuṭaja* tree.

Furthermore, it has been stated that even a cognition arising at the culmination of the intensification of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), though appearing as immediate, is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its fallibility.
The objector summarizes his own position: "Therefore, if...
The objector states another objection: "And not when [the means] have operated once.
Indeed, a certain person of pure nature—like Vāmadeva while still in the womb—hearing and reflecting, and having focused for a moment, realizes the identity of the individual self with Brahman.
"Furthermore, repetition would be purposeless.

Therefore, repetition is purposeless because there is either the apprehension or the non-apprehension of that which is partless; it is not a matter of being manifest or unmanifest, as is the case with universals and particulars, or like rubies and the like. To this he says: "Moreover, [it is] manifold-parted. He provides the resolution: "To this it is replied: Repetition might indeed be purposeless."

This is the intended meaning: it is true that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is not the immediate fruit of scripture and reasoning; rather, it is the mind itself—assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the knowledge of the meaning of reasoning and scripture—that stabilizes the cognitive modification (*buddhivṛtti*) directed toward the direct realization of Brahman.

And this [realization] is not invalid as a form of intuitive perception (*prātibha*), like the direct realization of fire inferred through logic, because at that time the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire is indeed present to the senses; for the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the very nature of Brahman conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is always an immediacy (*aparokṣatva*).
For purity, buddhahood, and so forth do not, in reality, exceed that [Brahman].
Rather, it is understood that the *jīva* itself, when devoid of its respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is Brahman by nature as purity and the rest.
Nor does the absence of those respective limiting adjuncts exceed that [Brahman].

Therefore, just as one who has acquired the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the study of the knowledge of the science of music perceives the distinctions among the scales (*grāma*), melodies (*mūrcchanā*), and notes such as *ṣaḍja* through the ear aided by a teacher,

so too does one who has acquired the mental impressions from the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedāntas perceive the nature of Brahman in the individual soul (*jīva*) through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
This applies even to one for whom the statement "That thou art" has been uttered but once.
"Having heard, having reflected, and having concentrated for a moment" means due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by practice in previous lives.
"But he who is unable" means one who is devoid of the practice of Brahman in previous lives.

For it is never observed that something which is logically possible is impossible. The point is this: since even in the case of a sentence-meaning that appears indirectly (parokṣa), there exists a gradation of clarity and obscurity, what need is there to speak of the gradation of clarity in a stream of cognitions that culminates in direct perception (sākṣātkāra)—a stream produced by the sequence of increasing intensity in the practice of meditative absorption (ādhyāsa) following upon reflection (manana)? The sense is as follows: when even the meaning of a verbal statement, which is not directly perceived, manifests with varying degrees of clarity and lack of clarity, then what can be said regarding the gradations of manifestation in a continuous flow of cognition that arises from the progressive refinement of the practice of meditative absorption after the stage of reflection, and which has direct realization as its limit? In such a case, the existence of such gradations is self-evident.
Thus, it has been stated that even regarding the meaning of a sentence in general, comprehension does not occur instantaneously.

However, the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)—whose constituent word-meanings are exceedingly difficult to grasp—does not immediately lead to the knowledge of its own overall meaning prior to the knowledge of those word-meanings.

Rather, because the knowledge of its word-meanings is most delayed, the comprehension of the sentence occurs with extreme delay; thus he says: "Furthermore, as for this sentence 'That thou art,' [it relates] to the meaning of the word *tvam*... and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), consisting of the connection of word-meanings (*padārtha-saṃsarga*), is appropriately perceived as having a sequence because its determination depends upon the sequence of the cognitions of those word-meanings. However, Brahman—being partless and thus devoid of unconnected, manifold word-meanings—is such that there could be no sequential perception of anything; it was therefore said that it must either be grasped all at once or not grasped at all. To this, he says: "And although the Self to be realized is partless... [and so forth].

Although the Self is partless and directly perceived, through the removal and superimposition of this or that body and so forth, it appears as if possessed of parts and as if entirely beyond perception.
Consequently, its realization as the meaning of a sentence is logically established as a process of successive cognitions.

Now, one might ask: "Is this very cognition produced by the sentence [the final realization] regarding the Self? And if so, there would be no direct perception of the Self, because this [sentence-generated cognition] has not yet reached its fruit. To this he says: "But that is merely the prior form of the realization of the Self."
[This refers to] that which possesses direct realization.

This is what is meant: meditation (*bhāvanā*)—which follows upon hearing and reflecting on the meaning of the sentence and which possesses three qualifications—is capable of bringing about the direct realization of Brahman; thus, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is the precursor to direct realization.
He raises an objection: "True, it is so.
For superimposition (samāropa) is indeed sublated by the cognition of reality (tatvapratyaya), but the cognition of reality itself is not [sublated].

Since the cognition of suffering and so forth arises in everyone at all times with respect to the Self, it is valid because it is unsublated; thus, being powerful, it cannot be removed—this is the meaning.
He refutes this: "No;
[it is] like the conceit of being the body and so forth.
For it is not because something arises for everyone at all times that it possesses ultimate reality.
Otherwise, it would follow that the identification of the body with the self is also real, and thus it too would arise for everyone at all times.
Yet, as has been stated in various places through logical reasoning, that [identification] is indeed sublated; the same applies to the identification with suffering and so forth.
For suffering, grief, and the like—which possess the nature of arising and passing away—cannot possibly be the self, whose nature is eternally pure and enlightened.

Nor are they [the atoms] the properties (dharma) of those [compounds], because it is logically impossible for things that are absolutely distinct from them to possess them as their properties; for a cow is not the property of a horse. Furthermore, the relationship itself cannot withstand analysis, whether it be considered as distinct or non-distinct [from its relata], and whether it be considered as connected or unconnected [to them]. Moreover, since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, they cannot coexist in a single locus.
All of this has been established in the second chapter.
This is what was stated: "Because, like the body and so forth, they are perceived as external to consciousness.
Furthermore, he says "and in states such as deep sleep" to show that suffering and the rest do not have identity [with the Self].
This might be the case:

why is repetition accepted solely for the sake of direct experience, when by such injunctions as "it is to be seen" and "it is to be heard," repetition would be prescribed with reference to something other than the subject matter of the sentence "That thou art"? To this he says: "Even there, not from the meaning of the sentence 'That thou art'."
In the passage beginning with "The Self, verily, my dear, is to be seen," the vision of the Self is enjoined.

Furthermore, no vision of the Self other than that which has the sentence "That thou art" as its object is recorded in scripture; for that which is introduced at the beginning and concluded at the end constitutes the meaning of the sentence.
Since [the Upanishad] begins with "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning" and concludes with "That thou art," that alone is the meaning of the sentence.
Therefore, by excluding [the bridegroom] from this [act] and assigning him elsewhere, one destroys the primary element with its subordinate part.
For the bridegroom (*vara*), being intended as the recipient of the action, is the primary *saṃpradāna* (recipient);
they do not obstruct him with the act of marriage, which is merely a subordinate part of the ritual action.

Now, it might be objected that because the sentence has injunction (*vidhi*) as its primary purport, it does not have an existent fact (*bhūtārtha*) as its primary purport; rather, the existent fact is conveyed only as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to that injunction.

As they say while explaining the Śabara-bhāṣya passage beginning with "For an injunction [conveys] what is existent and what is coming into being": "An injunction, while making known a purposeful task (*kārya*), makes known what is existent and so forth as being subordinate to that [task]. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "And for one who is enjoined in this [rite], [there arises the thought]: 'I am authorized.'"

Just as it has been established in the sūtra "But that [Brahman, because of the harmony of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*) that the Vedāntas terminate in the reality of things (*bhūtārtha*) and do not culminate in injunctions of action (*kāryavidhi*), on the contrary, if they were to culminate in injunction, they would produce cognitions opposed to liberation and would thus destroy liberation; this [point] mentioned here is merely an additional argument. //2//
START BsVBh_4,1.2.3:
However, they accept [the existence of] a self and cause others to grasp it. BBs_4,1.3:
Even though such scriptural passages as "That thou art" establish that the transmigrating soul possesses the nature of the Supreme Self, nevertheless...
Because their difference is determined by the association of contradictory attributes— such as being free from evil versus not being free from evil—
and because of scriptural texts such as "That thou art," and "The mind is Brahman," and "The sun is Brahman."
Since this is also logically consistent as being intended to teach a mere symbol (pratīka), as in the aforementioned examples, this is indeed an instruction regarding a symbol.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to argue that, just as the nature of a rope present before one is enjoined by restating the superimposed nature of a snake, so too the state of the Supreme Self is enjoined by restating the individual selfhood of the luminous Self.

For it is indeed logical that when a substance present before one is perceived in its general form but not grasped in its specific form, there occurs the superimposition of another specific quality. In this case, however, since the nature of light is a featureless generality whose illumination is independent of anything else, there is no aspect whatsoever that remains ungrasped; thus, upon the non-grasping of what specific quality could what other specific quality be superimposed?

Therefore, since the superimposition of the state of being a living soul (jīva) onto Brahman is impossible, it follows that the teaching "That thou art" is merely an instruction regarding a symbolic representation (pratīka), such as "The living soul is Brahman" or "Brahman is the living soul."
This being the case, it is replied: Śvetaketu’s very self is to be understood as the Supreme Lord, and not a Supreme Lord distinct from Śvetaketu.
For if there were a difference, it would result in a figurative sense, and a figurative sense is not appropriate when a primary sense is possible.
Moreover, in the case of an instruction regarding a symbol (*pratīka*), a single mention is perceived, as well as a censure of the perception of difference.
For in repetition, there is an increase in the meaning, not a diminution; nor does it become figurative when it is far removed [from its primary sense].
Therefore, by examining the preceding and following passages of the scripture, it is observed that its purport is that the identity of the individual soul with the Supreme Self is real.

Nor is there a lack of authority for the Śruti here due to contradiction with other means of knowledge (*māna*); indeed, all such points regarding the absence of contradiction with other means of knowledge have already been established in the first chapter. Furthermore, although [the Self] is partless, because a certain "part" as it were—consisting of the manifold phenomenal world superimposed by beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*) and its latent impressions—is not grasped, there is what appears to be an error; however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no error at all.

There is no such thing as "name" nor is there anything called "saṃsāra. Rather, we consider it logical that all this is indefinable because it is the locus of every kind of impossibility. With this intention, it was said: "If you are thus bound, there is no one who is not awakened."
Others also say: "If there is no satisfaction in non-duality, you are liberated at all times. This other [verse] has a meaning that goes beyond [the previous one]. //3//
Not in a symbol, for he is not that.

Just as it is taught in the scriptures, Brahman— whose nature is pure and liberated— is to be meditated upon by the individual soul (*jīva*) precisely as the Self, [in the realization] "I am Brahman."

In passages such as "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," for what reason [is this taught]? Because the individual soul (jīvātman) is essentially identical with Brahman, and because of the scriptural teaching that [Brahman] is non-dual.

Just as the individual souls are reflections of Brahman upon the mirror of ignorance, so too, wherever there is an instruction to view the mind or the sun as Brahman, in all such cases one should perceive Brahman as "I am the mind" and so forth.
"Selfhood is primary.
And it is logical that the mind and the other faculties possess identity [with Brahman] by virtue of being its transformations (*vikāra*),
just as jars, bowls, buckets, and the like— which are transformations of clay— possess the nature of clay.

And thus, since it is understood from certain such symbolic instructions (*pratīkopadeśa*) that some modification is dissolved, it follows that their purpose is solely the dissolution of the manifold of difference (*bheda-prapañca*).

To this, it is replied: Just as in passages such as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), the identity of Brahman with the locus of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is taught, so too in passages such as "The mind is Brahman" (*mano brahma*), the status of being the locus of the ego is not taught for the mind and other [organs].
However, these [organs] are to be meditated upon as Brahman.

If it is argued that, since the locus of the "I" (ahaṅkāra) is Brahman, one should meditate on the mind and other organs—which are to be meditated upon as Brahman—as being the locus of the "I," we say no;
because in such passages, the word "I" (aham) is not heard.

If, however, one were to conceive of [the elements] as the locus of the *ahaṃkāra* by virtue of their being the Self of Brahman, then—just as in the case of its reflection—it would follow that other modifications of it, such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, must also be meditated upon within the mind and the other organs.

Therefore, when meditation on something as having the nature of a particular [element] is enjoined, it should be understood only as having that specific nature, according to the maxim: "What is stated [in scripture] is only as far as the statement goes.
Nothing more should be superimposed, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the dissolution of the entire collection of sentences—that is, the phenomenal world—is not the intended purpose [of this teaching].

For if that were the goal, the mention of the "mind" (*manas*) as a representative symbol (*pratīka*) would be useless; one should have said "the universe" (*viśvam*), just as in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman.
Nor is it appropriate for the mention of the mind to serve as a mere illustration of the whole.
For when the primary meaning is possible, it is improper to resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
furthermore, this would result in the futility of such passages as "The sun is Brahman. Indeed, the worshiper does not [identify with] the symbols themselves.
The meaning is that there is neither experience of the adjuncts (pratīka), such as the mind and so forth, as the Self, nor is there any scriptural statement to that effect; for otherwise,
it would follow that the adjuncts themselves would cease to exist.

[Objection: "But surely, just as there is the non-existence of that which is limited—the locus of the 'I'-notion—by virtue of its being the Self of the unlimited Brahman, so too will it be for the symbols (pratīka). To this, he says: "And because of the sublation of the essential nature of name and the rest.
For here, the symbols are intended to be enjoined as primary objects of meditation by way of being the locus of the 'I'-notion.
However, in passages such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), the locus of the 'I'-notion is not understood to be the object of meditation.
However, just as the true nature of the rope is made known by means of the description of the snake, the dissolution of that which is limited—the locus of the ego—is understood here.
What follows from this if it is so?
This is what follows: the destruction of the primary counter-objects (pratīkas) is not logical, nor is their destruction compatible with the performance of the enjoined rite.
Furthermore, it is not the case that [the injunctions regarding meditation] are based on Brahman being the Self.

For the injunctions for meditation do not form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the textual passages such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), which are intent upon establishing the identity of the individual self (*jīvātman*) with the nature of Brahman;

otherwise, by virtue of being part of that same sentence, one might assume the view of the Self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) in those teachings where the view of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) is instructed. This is because they belong to different contexts (*bhinnaprakaraṇatvāt*).

And thus, since in that context the individual soul (jīva)—established according to worldly perception—is the agent, the enjoyer, and the transmigrator, and not Brahman, how can the vision of the Self be taught in those instructions regarding the vision of Brahman through the identity of that soul with Brahman? This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is because the meditator is equal [in nature] to the symbols (pratīka).
Even though the meditator, being the individual soul, is not a modification (vikāra) of Brahman, [the meditation on the symbol as Brahman is still possible].

The symbols, however, consist of the mind and so forth; although they are modifications of Brahman, they should nevertheless be regarded as being similar to the individual self (jīvātman) by virtue of their limited nature. //4//
"BSBh_4,1.4.5 The view of Brahman [is to be applied to the sun] because of its superiority.

BSBh_4,1.5 Although grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible in both ways, nevertheless, because Brahman is the presiding lord of all and possesses the capacity to produce the fruit [of liberation], [it is superior]."

Because it possesses fruit, that [Brahman] alone should be refined primarily by means of the meditations (*dṛṣṭi*) upon the sun and so forth; thus, the meditations on the sun and so forth must be applied to Brahman itself, but not the meditation on Brahman to the sun and so forth. Furthermore, when the meaning of the scripture has been thus determined, the worldly maxim that "the vision of the inferior [is superimposed] upon the superior" is not capable of subverting it, because that very maxim is set aside due to its contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āgama*). This is the summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is true that, because it is the presiding witness of all and the bestower of the fruit, Brahman alone possesses actual primacy everywhere; nevertheless, in accordance with the course of the words [of the Veda], in certain instances the primacy of the ritual action (*karman*) alone is determined,
as for example in such [injunctions] as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā."

For it has been established here that in all cases, it is the deity alone, propitiated by sacrifices and other rites, who bestows the fruit; nevertheless, because the action is understood from the word itself to be the instrument (*karaṇa*), it possesses primacy through the perception of its being the means to the fruit.
In some instances, however, the material substance (*dravya*) possesses primacy, as in "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and so forth.
As it has been said: "In those cases where the substance is intended to be thoroughly prepared, there the subordinate factor (*guṇa*) is perceived."

Thus, although in reality Brahman alone, as the universal supervisor, bestows the fruit, nevertheless the scripture declares that when a symbol such as the sun is meditated upon with the thought that it is Brahman, Brahman becomes the means for the attainment of the fruit;

or alternatively, that it is Brahman itself, when made the object of meditation through the cognition of the sun and so forth, that leads to the fruit. In either case, the granting of the fruit by Brahman—the universal supervisor—is logically established.
When there is doubt regarding the meaning of a treatise, it is determined in accordance with worldly usage.
This is what was stated: "Once the meaning of the treatise has been determined, it must be so.

Not only is worldly logic the cause for such determination, but also the fact that words such as "Āditya" possess their primary (literal) meaning due to being mentioned first; thus he says: "And because of being first."
Thus, the fact that the word *brahman* is followed by the particle *iti* leads one to understand this very same principle.

To explain: just as words such as *āditya* (sun) function in their own primary sense through the application of their own accentuation, so too the word *brahman* will function in its own primary sense if its own meaning is intended here. If that were the case, the use of *iti* would be purposeless; therefore, having displaced the word *brahman* from its own primary meaning, it must be made to refer either to knowledge (*jñāna*) or to the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Nor is the word "Brahman" the referent of the sun and so forth;
rather, this word "iti" is used solely for the purpose of indicating a cognition, just as in the expression, "The gavaya occurred to me as a cow.
Thus, the meaning becomes that the sun and others are to be understood as Brahman; he states this by saying, "also because of the word 'Brahman' being followed by 'iti'."
The remainder has its meaning not hidden [and is thus self-evident]. //5//
And the cognitions of the sun and so forth [are to be applied] to the subsidiary parts [of the sacrifice], because that is logical;
or rather, the cognitions of the *udgītha* and so forth must necessarily be superimposed upon the sun and so forth.

Even though the sun and other such entities exist, because the fruit is not produced [from them] and because the fruit is seen to arise from action alone, which possesses the capacity for production, action itself is what possesses the fruit.

Thus, if the rites such as the Udgītha were made the objects of the meditations on the sun and so forth, then those forms of the rites would be overwhelmed by the perceptions of the sun and other such objects.
And in this way, how could a fruit arise from ritual forms that are merely conceptual?

On the other hand, when the sun and so forth are meditated upon through the perception of the *udgītha* and so on, those suns and others—being of the nature of ritual action when viewed through the cognition of the *udgītha* and so forth—will be fit for the production of the fruit.

For this very reason, the application of the terms *ṛk* and *sāman* to the earth and fire is justified, since the perception of the *ṛk* is superimposed upon the earth and the perception of the *sāman* upon fire.
Furthermore, if the fire were meditated upon in the *sāman* and the earth in the *ṛc*, it would be the reverse;
therefore, he says that this [former view] alone is logical: "And thus, this very [one]... He states another supporting argument: "Moreover, in the worlds..."

Thus, this reference to the preceding section is appropriate as being intended to establish the status of the objects [of meditation], provided that the vision of the Sāman is superimposed upon the worlds and not otherwise.
He states the justification for the conclusion of the previous section regarding this very point: "And in the case of those first mentioned.
He now introduces the established conclusion (siddhānta) here: "The cognitions of Āditya and so forth alone [are to be superimposed]."

For that which is enjoined or prohibited by the scripture for the sake of a result or for the avoidance of misfortune—such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice and the like, or the killing of a Brahmin and the like—possesses an intermediate operation consisting of an *apūrva* (unseen potency).

Since this matter stands thus by the force of logic—that the designation "like a lotus leaf," and so forth, must be explained as being intended solely for the praise of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā)—the following is said in response: This designation would indeed be explained in such a manner if there were a contradiction with the injunctions regarding ritual action (karma-vidhi), but such a contradiction does not exist.

For the scripture (śāstra) makes known only the capacity of rituals to produce results; it does not, however, establish that this capacity is unimpeded by any adventitious cause, such as the need for expiation (prāyaścitta).
Because the scripture is indifferent to that matter:

if the capacity of a karma to produce its result, as taught by the scripture, is unobstructed by any adventitious karma, then it will indeed produce that result, and thus there is no contradiction with the scripture.
Furthermore, the traditional teaching (smṛti) stating "karma that has not been experienced does not perish" refers to karma whose capacity has been obstructed.

Furthermore, there is a scriptural injunction for the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) to remove defects, similar to the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because there is no difference in their connection with both [the removal of defects and the attainment of sovereignty].

Even in the case of the higher knowledge that is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇā paravidyā*), where there is no explicit mention of the removal of defects, the capacity to produce their destruction is determined simply by reflecting upon its essential nature.

For it is not possible that a living being (*jīva*), whose delusions such as agency and enjoyership have been entirely wiped away by the meditative cultivation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) arising from the contemplation of the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), would still be joined with the experience of results.
Indeed, fear, trembling, and the like—which are based on the superimposition of a snake upon a rope—do not persist once there is direct realization of the reality of the rope;
rather, even though they may continue for some time due to the residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), they certainly cease.

Confirming this very point, designations such as "like a lotus leaf" and so forth, being consistent with their literal meaning, do not deserve to be explained away in any way as mere figurative praise.

Now, it might be argued: "It has been stated that there will be such a state of the living self (jīvātman) in which, either through sequential enjoyment or by the power of yogic perfection (*yogarddhi*) through the simultaneous creation of multiple bodies, a being—by enjoying [the fruits] non-sequentially—will exhaust his *karma*s and become liberated. To this, he says: "And in this very way, liberation is logically possible."

Furthermore, it is because the fruit of knowledge cannot be something beyond perception.
Liberation is indeed accepted as the fruit of knowledge.
And the immediate fruit of knowledge is the manifestation of the object of knowledge;

If it were assumed that the fruit of liberation for knowledge arises through a succession of unseen impressions (*apūrva*), then knowledge would have a non-evident fruit and its purpose would be invisible (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). And the meaning is that when a visible result is possible, the postulation of an invisible one is not logical.
Therefore, it is established that when Brahman is attained—that is, when there is knowledge of Brahman and non-duality is realized—there is the destruction of evil. //13//

Since the path beginning with smoke is not so qualified, it must lead to a different result. Prior to the direct realization of the meaning of the sentence "That thou art," it is indeed logical that the individual soul—though in reality unconditioned, yet appearing as if conditioned due to the limitations of adjuncts such as ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—conceives itself to be different from others in the world and attains through movement those worlds, such as the Path of Light (*arcis*), which are other than its own nature and not yet reached.

However, for one who possesses the direct realization of the non-dual reality of Brahman, whose delusive appearance of the entire phenomenal world has dissolved, there is no destination, no going, and no one to lead; what, then, could be consistent with what?

If it is argued that, just as even for a wise man of steady wisdom (*sthitaprajña*) prior to the fall of the body, the persistence of worldly attributes is admitted as a mere appearance, so too for the wise man until the fall of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), there persists the persistence of those attributes; and thus, because he has not yet attained what was unattained, the occurrence of movement [to Brahman] is logical, and upon reaching that place, liberation occurs through the cessation of the subtle body, on the authority of scripture—[we reply:

no, because for one possessing the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), departure [from the body] is prohibited by such texts as: "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman; his vital breaths do not depart from him; they are merged right here."

Indeed, when ignorance has been completely uprooted by the direct realization of the identity of the individual self with Brahman—which arises from the constant contemplation "All this is indeed Brahman, I am Brahman"—there remains nothing further to be done.

For one devoid of faith, ritual acts whose results are visible in this world sometimes bear fruit and sometimes do not.

If, however, it depends on Supreme Knowledge, does this cultivation of the path provide assistance toward the effect of that Knowledge, or toward the arising of that Knowledge?

First of all, [knowledge] does not function as an auxiliary to knowledge itself, because it is impossible for them to coexist due to their mutual contradiction, since they have respectively the domains of duality and non-duality.

Therefore, in accordance with the numerous scriptural citations presented and on the grounds of logical consistency, the word *brahman*—whose primary sense is impossible here—must be understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the lower Brahman due to its proximity to Brahman.

This is because the use of the plural number in the phrase "in the worlds" (*lokeṣu*) is thus justified, as it refers to the world of the effected (lower) Brahman; for the supreme [Brahman], being partless, such a designation is impossible even by way of that [world].

If the term "world" (*loka*) were understood—as it is conventionally established—to mean a specific arrangement of matter serving as a ground for experience, like the earth encircled by the *celā* mountains and so forth, then it could not in any way be explained through yoga as referring to the Light (*prakāśa*).
Therefore, it is established that the venerable Bādarāyaṇa is one who perceives correctly, whereas Jaimini is one who does not perceive correctly.

The many prattlings of those who lack authoritative means of knowledge—such as the claim that the qualities of an all-pervading substance must themselves be all-pervading, including consciousness, bliss, and so forth—are merely idle chatter.

Arguments such as "the qualities of the Supreme Self possess both difference and non-difference" have been left aside by us, for even when restated for the sake of refutation, they bring about a lack of authoritative proof.

As for the construction of the text: because the travelers [the individual souls] are the inner self (*pratyagātman*), Brahman—which is called *pratyak* because it moves toward (*añcati*) each and every object, thus existing within every entity—is their very self; this refers to the individual selves who are the travelers.
The statement "but it is figurative elsewhere" refers to other cases.
For even the etymological sense is merely secondary (gauṇī) in view of the quality of yoga.
Regarding the phrase "connected with pure limiting adjuncts" (viśuddhopādhisaṃbandham):
mental constructions such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth are to be understood as effects [of those adjuncts].
Although they are impure because they are effects (*kāryatva*), they are pure because they are causes of the highest good (*śreyas*).

"Return" (*pratisaṃcara*) refers to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). "Practice" (*pratipatti*) refers to the intention to practice (*abhisaṃdhi*); it is "practice" (*gati*) because the root *pad* has the meaning of "going. "Intention" (*abhisaṃdhi*) means purpose (*tātparya*).

[This is understood] by breaking the previous sentence,

The analogy of the banyan tree and the monkey has been established; [the author] refutes it, saying:

This is the intended meaning: whereas the Nyagrodha tree as a whole undergoes transformation by being joined with conjunctions and disjunctions born of karma— which possess the nature of arising and passing away— this Supreme Self, however, from whom the entire manifold of difference has been eliminated and who is immutable and eternal,

However, imagined conjunction and disjunction are possible only for the imagined world of the effect-Brahman, not for the Supreme [Brahman].

Therefore, by both scripture and reasoning, this sacred tradition is intent upon propounding Brahman as devoid of all distinctions, and not intent upon propounding [the world's] origination and so forth.
Consequently, movement is not ultimately real.

namely, the two positions regarding parts and modification based on whether [the mover] is other or non-other than [the body],

Now, why is absolute non-difference not postulated? To this he says: "Because of absolute identity. For entities such as jars and the like, which are modifications, are pervaded by the nature of clay as their own essence;

Furthermore, on the two views that [the transmigrating entity] is either a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*) [of Brahman], movement characterized by *saṃsāra* is untenable for Brahman, because Brahman—possessing those modifications and parts—is stable and immovable.
Indeed, that which is stable by nature cannot become unstable.
Moreover, the sense is that even if one were to argue they are both different and non-different, it is impossible due to the contradiction inherent in a single entity being both.

Regarding the phrase "having a medium magnitude":
this is because one observes that things of medium magnitude, such as jars and the like, are impermanent. [The opponent replies: "No; [it refers to] primary oneness."
Since the contradictory states of difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one place, there must be a difference in the object itself due to the difference in cognition and designation.

Furthermore, under the views that the individual souls (jīvas) are either parts of Brahman, modifications of it, or entirely distinct from it, transmigratory existence would be real. Consequently, upon liberation, because they would have to abandon their essential nature, it would follow that the souls themselves are destroyed.

But if [the world] is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, then Brahman alone is the nature of these [individual souls], just as the original object (*bimba*) is the nature of its reflections; and since that [Brahman] is indestructible, there is no destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*). He introduces another view in order to refute it: "As for what is prattled by some—that the obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karmāṇi*) [are effective] even without the knowledge of Brahman.

For just as a fever caused by phlegm (*kapha*), once the accumulated phlegm has been diminished by specific treatments and so forth, does not recur even when it has subsided, provided one avoids curd and other things that cause the production of further phlegm—so too [is the case with ritual action].

Thus, bondage caused by karma ceases when the accumulated karmas are exhausted through experience; and because there is no performance of other karmas—which are the causes of bondage—the effect cannot arise in the absence of its cause. Consequently, due to the absence of bondage, liberation is established by its very nature, like health.
Furthermore, by performing obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites for the destruction of accumulated evil, the transgression caused by that evil does not occur.
And since no transgression arises, one whose mind is at ease should not practice what is prohibited;
this [position] he refutes as follows: "That is incorrect, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence."

"Indeed, the scripture is the authority in this matter, and it teaches that for one seeking liberation, self-knowledge alone [is required], not the aforementioned conduct. Nor does reasoning prevail here, because since saṃsāra is beginningless, the accumulation of karma is also incalculable and its time of fruition is indefinite; thus, it is impossible to exhaust it through experience. To this he says: "And this cannot even be reasoned about," and he raises an objection: "It might be so..."
Regarding the word "eternal" (*nitya*), he provides the rebuttal: "That is not so, because there is no contradiction.

For if obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites were to exhaust even well-performed merit (*sukṛta*) just as they do evil (*duṣkṛta*), it would follow that the injunctions for optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) would be rendered utterly useless.
Indeed, there is no one among the four castes or the four stages of life who does not perform obligatory and occasional rites;
therefore, these [rites] do not conflict with merit.
He states this as a further elaboration: "Nor [is there conflict] from the performance of obligatory and occasional rites."
"And it is not so when right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is absent.

For one who possesses right vision is dispassionate; even while avoiding actions that are desirable or prohibited, he exhausts those that have arisen through negligence by means of that very right vision.
Furthermore, when knowledge has reached maturity, he simply does not act [further]. But an ignorant person, though clever, acts out of negligence.
Furthermore, it is impossible to destroy [these qualities] once they have been produced; this is the distinction.

Moreover, if the identity of Brahman and the Self is not accepted as being accessible through knowledge, and if agency and enjoyership—along with the actions and experiences they entail—are determined to be the very nature of the Self rather than being superimposed, then they cannot be removed.

For an entity cannot be deprived of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because that would entail the destruction of the entity itself. Nor can an experience that possesses an existent intrinsic nature be made non-existent;
indeed, even Śakra could not turn blue into non-blue. Thus it has been said: "Because intrinsic nature is unavoidable."

The point is this: it is possible for the nature of that which is superimposed—which is inexpressible—to be removed by the knowledge of reality, just as the [superimposed] snake is [removed] by the knowledge of the rope's true nature.
Not understanding this point, an opponent objects: "This may be so;
however, agency and enjoyership are effects."
One who holds the view that [the self] is not manifest refutes what was just said with the words "And that is not so.

"Bādarāyaṇa maintains that [the Lord] leads even those who have the non-pratīka as their support, because there would be faults in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve (tatkratu).

For there exist meditations on symbols (pratīka), such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and so forth.

Those who possess these [meditations] are also entitled to go by way of the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi), just like those who meditate on the effected Brahman (kārya-brahma). This is because it has been established, without distinction, that the going applies to other meditations as well in the rule: "There is no restriction for all [meditations].
Nor is it the case that for these [practitioners of symbol-meditations], as for those who know the supreme Brahman, going is impossible.

Nor is it an absolute rule that only those whose sacrificial rites (*kratu*) are directed toward Brahman attain the world of Brahman, while those whose rites are not so directed do not; for even those who know the five fires (*pañcāgnividaḥ*), though their rites are not directed toward Brahman, nevertheless attain it.

Furthermore, these [meditations] are not devoid of being rites directed toward Brahman, because in all such cases—as in "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and so forth—there is the accompaniment of Brahman, and thus the status of having Brahman as one's sacrificial aim (*tatkratutva*) is possible.
Since a distinction in the fruit is possible even in the attainment of the world of Brahman—

given that it possesses parts and thus admits of degrees of excellence and deficiency— this being the position reached, the following reply is given: "Because of the progressive increase [of the fruit] up to the state of having Brahman as one's resolve, the nameless ones lead those who meditate on the symbol to the world of Brahman."

Let it be that even those who do not perform sacrifices dedicated to Brahman (*abrahmakratu*) are led to the world of Brahman through the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), because of the scriptural statement.

For what indeed can a scriptural statement not accomplish? There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement; however, in this case, since such a statement is absent, an exception (*apavāda*) is not tenable, because of the general rule of the scripture: "In whatever manner one meditates upon Him, that very thing one becomes. Thus, in the absence of a specific statement to the contrary, an exception is not justified.
Moreover, the worshiper of a symbol does not meditate upon Brahman— even though there is the accompaniment of the word "Brahman"—
but rather upon a specific particularity such as Name and so forth, in the form of Brahman. For thus, this [meditation] has Name and so forth as its primary basis, not Brahman as its primary basis.
The elders maintain that a "pratīka" is the projection of a cognition whose basis is one thing onto another basis.
Since the cognition whose basis is Brahman is projected onto names and so forth, it is dependent on the name (*nāmatantra*).
Therefore, the worshiper of such a pratīka does not have Brahman as their object of meditation (*brahmakratu*), but rather has the name and so forth as their object of meditation (*nāmādikratu*).

Furthermore, since those who meditate on names and so forth are not distinct in their status as having Brahman as their object of sacrifice (*brahmakratu*), a progressive superiority among them is not possible.
Nor is Brahman itself a "sacrifice" whose constituent parts would constitute sacrifices such that superiority could be described in relation to those parts.
Therefore, excluding those wise ones who take symbols (*pratīka*) as their support, the non-human being leads all others who take modifications (*vikāra*) as their support to the world of Brahman.

For there is no fault whatsoever in accepting that this dual nature exists when the meaning is twofold—namely, that [the path] does not lead some who rely on the symbols (pratīka) but does lead those wise ones who rely on the modifications (vikāra)—in accordance with the principle that "there is no restriction for all [meditations]. Thus, everything is clear. //15//

Since agency belongs to that which was previously non-existent in order to bring about its production, and not to that which already exists;
and since liberation is established as being a fruit, it must involve the emergence of a different form.
The production of something like a jar is the becoming of what was previously non-existent, but not the becoming of that which is either absolutely existent or absolutely non-existent.
A sky-flower is never produced.
If liberation were the abiding of the self in its own nature, it would not be produced, because that [self], being as utterly non-existent as the sky, lacks prior non-existence.
Furthermore, its state of being free from bondage is not established, because that which has the nature of a void would necessarily follow as being non-void by virtue of being an effect.

Moreover, since liberation is well-known to be a fruit, it is impossible for that which is not an effect to be a fruit; thus, if it were produced through some adventitious form, [it would be an effect].
Regarding the point that "by [the word] *svena*" refers back to what has already been established, it is replied: For when meaningfulness is possible, meaninglessness is not accepted;
rather, the single nature of bondage is distinguished by its existence or non-existence.

For verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) is indeed a means of valid cognition that brings about the understanding of what has not been previously apprehended; it is only described as a restatement (*anuvāda*) in some way due to the absence of any other recourse.

However, when it brings about the understanding of the serene nature of the self—which is devoid of all worldly phenomena and is distinct from that very same [worldly] nature which is not serene—it is not logical for it to be a restatement, because it makes known what was previously unapprehended.
Nor is its realization impossible.
For just as in the case of a jar or similar object, the accomplishment of the cessation of bondage is established for worldly practice through conventional means of valid cognition;
however, the lack of establishment due to being unable to withstand critical analysis is equal in both cases.
Indeed, it has been stated more than once that what is non-existent cannot arise.

It would either be like the nature of the self, or its nature would have to be differentiated,
because it is non-different from the differentiated [parts], just like the forms of blue and yellow.
Nor is it tenable to claim that the attributes do not differ from the substrate (the self) while differing among themselves;
for, due to their non-difference from the substrate, they too would necessarily be non-different.
Or else, if there were difference [among them], it would follow that the substrate itself must also be different, as has already been stated.

It has been established in the first Sūtra that difference and non-difference cannot coexist in a single locus due to their mutual contradiction. Furthermore, although things of the nature of non-existence do not obstruct non-duality, since evil and the like are conceptual (*kālpnika*) and are defined in dependence upon that [non-duality], they too are conceptual; thus, a real (*tāttvika*) attribution of those qualities does not apply.
By this, qualities such as having true desires, omniscience, and being the Lord of all are also explained as being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Therefore, Auḍulomi held that for the Self which, upon liberation, is manifested as pure consciousness alone—devoid of all phenomenal expansion (prapañca) and beyond verbal designation—the designations such as "free from evil," "possessing true desires," and so forth, are merely devoid of objective referents. This has been stated: these qualities, such as being free from evil, are born solely of the conceptual play of words (*śabdavikalpa*), and do not even exist at the level of conventional usage (*sāṃvyavahārika*). //6//
"Even so, because of this presentation, Bādarāyaṇa [holds] there is no contradiction due to prior existence.
This audacity of Auḍulomi is not tolerated by him (Bādarāyaṇa).
For the teacher Bādarāyaṇa, even while tolerating that view, [held a different opinion].
With the words "even so," he accords with the view of Auḍulomi;
however, he does not tolerate [his] arrogance, and thus says: "with regard to conventional usage.
This is what is meant: it is true that the self consists solely of ultimate bliss and consciousness.

The meaning is as follows: qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpman*) and having true desires (*satyakāma*), although not ultimately real because they are adventitious (*aupādhika*), are nonetheless established in the world through empirical means of knowledge (*vyāvahārikapramāṇa*); they are not absolutely non-existent, which would render the words expressing them unreal—like the expression "the head of Rāhu. //7//
"But [the creation of the world occurs] from volition alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
(BS 4.4.8) In the world, volition accomplishes an object without depending on external effort.
He was not seen there; rather, he was inferred from the swiftness of the effort.
For in the world, it is observed that one who desires to accomplish some purpose exerts effort; exerting himself, he strives; and striving, he attains that purpose—such is the sequence seen.
It is not the case that the desired object presents itself to him immediately after the mere wish.
Therefore, even by means of the Vedic revelation (śruti), which conforms to worldly practice, such a sequence must be accepted for the knower as well.

The restriction, however, that [the creation occurs] "from mere volition" (saṃkalpād eva) is made in view of the worldly weightiness of effort; for due to the power of knowledge, the effort of the knower is light. That which is light is as if non-existent.
This might be so.

Just as a woman brought forth by mere mental resolve serves as the cause for the emission of the final element for those who are lustful, so too will fathers and others, though brought forth by his own conceptualization, serve for their respective functions; therefore, he says: "and they are not produced by mere conceptualization alone.

For indeed, there are certain effects that must be accomplished by the actual nature of a thing, such as tooth-marks, jewel-strings, and so forth, which are accomplished by the actual thing that is a woman.
However, some [effects] are to be accomplished through knowledge, such as the emission of the final element (*caramadhātu*), horripilation (*romaharṣa*), and so forth, as previously described.

In that regard, when the father and others are brought forth by mere mental desire (*manoratha*), let those effects be accomplished by that knowledge alone; however, they ought not to be accomplished by the [actual] object itself.

For the jeweled necklaces and other such things, which are accomplished by an actual woman, do not arise for one who is lustful in the same way that horripilation and so forth arise [from the mere thought]. Regarding this, it is said: "When the full enjoyment is attained," it is replied: "The manifestation of the father and others..."
Because scripture declares that [the creation] proceeds from mere volition (saṃkalpa);
nor is there any sublation by inference here, since it is that very [inference] which is sublated by scripture.

For scripture (*śruti*), which makes its own object known independently of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be sublated by another means of valid cognition. In contrast, inference (*anumāna*) itself— requiring, as part of its own causal complex for its production, that its object not be sublated by another means of valid cognition, just like the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth— is sublated by scripture, which contradicts it, through the destruction of that [inferential] causal complex.
For this very reason, the inference regarding the purity of human skull-bones and the like is untenable, as its object is sublated by scripture.
Therefore, it is correct that for the wise, through the power of their knowledge, the presence of ancestors and others occurs by mere volition alone.
Thus say those who follow the scriptures: "Who indeed, apart from the power of yoga, drinks up the ocean like Agastya, or creates the Daṇḍaka forest like him?"
Therefore, everything is completely clear. //8//
And for this very reason, it has no other dominant influence (ananyādhipati).

For this very reason, the followers of the Purāṇas record that Saubhari, having manifested various bodies, sported simultaneously with the fifty daughters of Māndhātṛ.
And when the object is actually present, a mere eulogy cannot be considered purposeless.
And its meaningfulness is possible;

for although this [description] is recited in the context of the earthly knowledge (*bhaumavidyā*) as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), nevertheless, by means of this sovereignty belonging to the state possessing qualities (*saguṇāvasthā*), the very knowledge devoid of qualities is praised prior to that [earthly knowledge].
Moreover, a qualification does not function solely through the exclusion of connection with anything else.
Just as Caitra is an archer, so Jaimini considered that for those possessed of sovereign power, the conjunction of mind, body, and sense organs occurs necessarily. //11//
Bādarāyaṇa holds that both types [of departure] exist, as in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice; for he, being a proponent of non-restriction,

observes scriptural passages such as "by the mind alone" which refer to the domain of the mind only, and "he becomes onefold, he becomes threefold," which refer to the distinction between body and senses— whereas others are proponents of restriction.
It does not tolerate [the qualification] with the two preceding [terms],
because of conformity with the two types of scriptural tradition (*śruti*).
Furthermore, in such cases, a qualification is not understood as being intended merely to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

For since the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by men through the body and the mind-faculty (*manas*) is already established, there is no doubt regarding the connection with the mind; thus, the exclusion of that [connection] would be redundant.
However, the purposefulness of the established connection with the mind is understood through the restriction (*parisaṃkhyāna*) of it to something else.
Therefore, as in the expression "he sees with his left eye," here it is correct to understand it as an exclusion of connection with anything other than that.

"Like the twelve-day sacrifice": the status of the twelve-day sacrifice as a *satra* (sacrificial session) is understood from the injunction regarding sitting (*āsana*) and the practice of subsistence (*upāyi*), while its status as an *ahīna* (non-session) is understood when there is an injunction regarding the act of sacrificing (*yajati*).

By the injunction "those desiring supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) should undertake [the sacrifice] for twelve days," and by the statement "those who, knowing thus, undertake the sacrificial session (*sattra*"), it is understood that the twelve-day rite is a *sattra* involving many performers.

Likewise, by the injunction "one should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice with that very twelve-day rite," it is understood—due to the fixed number of performers—that it is an *ahīna*, just like the injunction "one should sacrifice with the two-night rite" (*dvirātra*).
Now, due to the absence of a body and sense organs, the wise one experiences a subtle enjoyment through the mind alone, as in a dream.
Why? Because of logical consistency; for there is the scriptural statement, "With the mind, he [sees] these.
If, on the other hand, there were no experience as in deep sleep, this scriptural statement would not be tenable.
Nor is there enjoyment as in the case of one possessing a body, because the appropriation of a body and so forth would be purposeless;
for enjoyment is complete only for one who possesses a body.
The phrase "because it is logical even here" should be supplied [to complete the argument].
This has been stated in two sūtras: "In the absence of a body, it is possible as in the state of deep sleep;
in its presence, it is like the waking state.
In the absence of a body, [the soul exists] as in the state of transition (sandhya), because it is logically possible;
in the presence of a body, it is as in the waking state.

"The entry [of the individual self] is like that of a lamp; for thus it is shown.

(BBs_4,4.15) Although this cognizing self (*vijñānātman*) is in reality non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it has attained the state of an individual soul (*jīva*) since beginningless time through its limitation by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is spatially restricted and imagined by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*).

Being limited in scope, he would not be able to simultaneously pervade other bodies— even those created by his own power— that exist in various locations, as long as he possesses an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
nor could he create another self.

If that which is being created were distinct from the creator, it would not be the Self; if it were the Self, then the relationship of agent and object could not exist, as difference is the basis for such a relation.

Nor does another internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) create it there, because that which is being created cannot have [another] internal organ as its limiting adjunct (upādhi). Indeed, this [Self] is already enclosed by the beginningless, innate internal organ, and thus it cannot now be connected with a present internal organ as its limiting adjunct.

Therefore, just as a wooden machine, being presided over by a conscious operator, conforms to his will, so too it might be argued that emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are likewise endowed with sense organs. To this, the following reply is given: "The status of being a body could never exist without being the locus of experience;
and since it is said that 'it is threefold,' the status of being a body is logically applicable even to the All-pervading One (*vibhu*)."

The scriptural passage stating, "He becomes threefold, fivefold, sevenfold, ninefold," and so forth, which describes the manifold state of the knower, is possible only when there is a connection with diverse limiting adjuncts (upādhis) consisting of bodies and sense organs; it does not apply to a difference in the cause that is the body itself.
For a chariot-driver, even when he has constructed various different machines and is operating them, is not designated as being manifold [on account of those machines].
Furthermore, the nature of being a body consists in being the locus of experience, and this is not applicable to machines, which are not loci of experience.
Therefore, he creates other bodies;
nor do those [bodies] function on the side of the body without being presided over by him.

Furthermore, for the wise one—who is omnipresent and whose ignorance has virtually dissolved—there is no such mastery over an innate internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as there is for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by virtue of which his innate internal organ would enter into a connection with another adventitious internal organ.
Therefore, it is logical that the wise one—

the controller of all, the Lord of all, whose resolve is true— having fashioned bodies together with their senses and internal organs, and having entered them in a single moment, dwells liberated in those worlds through each respective sense-organ and internal organ.

The illustration "like a lamp" (pradīpavat) means that the identity of a lamp is metaphorically attributed to individual lamps because there is a distinction between those existing on different wicks, which are distinct individuals.
In the same way, the meaning of the reflection is that the wise one—the individual self (jīvātman)—is one even when there is a difference of bodies.
"Following a single mind" means following a single intention. //15//
One who is perfected and solitary is called "liberated.

However, the possibility of such a state for him does not exist because it contradicts the Śruti; thus, he raises the point already discussed with the words, "But how [can there be liberation] for one who is liberated?
and "like water."

The form *salilaḥ* is derived from the nominal stem *salila-* by applying the suffix *kvip* in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāre*)—according to the rule *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ*—and then adding the suffix *ac* (as in the *pacādi* class).
What is meant is this: just as water poured into the ocean attains oneness with it, so too does the seer [attain oneness] with Brahman.
To this, the following Sūtra is given:
"With reference to either deep sleep or union [with the Supreme], for it is made manifest. (BS 4.4.16)
Among these, some scriptural passages refer to deep sleep, while others refer to "attainment" (sampatti), because that is the context;

however, the scriptural texts concerning lordly power (aiśvarya) refer to the state of fruition of knowledge with attributes (saguṇa-vidyā). As for the mention of liberation (mukti), it refers to that state [of attainment] being present, just as at twilight, when one sees the dawn-red, one speaks of "day. //16//
[The liberated soul] is excluded from the activity of governing the world, because of the context [of the passage] and because of its non-proximity [to such power]. On the other hand,
it may possess unrestrained power on account of scriptural texts concerning self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) and acting according to one's will (*kāmacāra*).
Even one whose own accomplishment depends upon God is a practitioner in this regard.

From such scriptural passages as "He attains self-sovereignty," "All the gods bring him tribute," and "He becomes one who moves at will in all worlds," it is understood that the sovereignty of the knower—like that of the Supreme Brahman—is independence from others.
Now, one might object: how can this sovereignty, obtained through the meditation on Brahman, be dependent on Brahman rather than being its very nature?
For entities whose birth is dependent upon a cause do not, in producing their own effects, require their own cause.
However, in this case, they are indeed independent.
As they have said: "A jar depends upon the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth for its birth;
but for the act of carrying water, it has no dependence on them."

Nor is it the case that because the wise possess the accomplishment of sovereignty dependent upon the Supreme Lord, their sovereignty is diminished in such a way that— just as worldly kings are subordinate to a Great King— the wise, while engaged in their own activities, would become subordinate to the Supreme Lord. Indeed, there is no rule whatsoever that the nature of a thing whose production is dependent on another must necessarily be inferior to that other's nature.
For we observe those who are equal to Him and even those who are superior; thus, a disciple is seen to be either equal to or superior to his teacher.
Furthermore, wicked vassals, whose sovereignty is dependent upon the king, are seen contending with kings or even conquering them.
Therefore, since the Supreme Lord possesses unsurpassed sovereignty, let it be that there are no wise men superior to Him; however, there may well be those who are His equals.
And thus, they are not dependent on one another;

for there is no mutual dependence among things that stand in a relationship of equal primacy. Therefore, being independent, they might proceed even in the act of creating the world. To this, it is replied: Because of their eternity, because of their independence, and also because of the Vedic revelation and its initial context.
And because of the unanimous consensus of the learned, the dependence upon the Supreme Lord is established.

For the effect characterized as the creation of the world must belong either to that which has the nature of the cause alone, or to that which has the nature of both cause and effect. In that case, since that which possesses both natures depends upon a root cause for its own production, one must accept that the already established Supreme Lord alone is the cause; therefore, let Him alone be the single cause of the world, because He, being eternal, does not depend on any cause of His own and possesses the requisite capacity.
The learned, however, possess the capacity for conceptualization regarding the creation of the world;
yet their status as creators of the world is not heard in scripture,
whereas that of the venerable Supreme Lord alone is so heard.
For all those scriptural texts proceed with reference to that very [single] primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, it is never observed that there is a uniform consensus among those who possess equal authority; thus, when one desires to create, the other would simultaneously desire to dissolve, resulting in creation and dissolution occurring without alternation.
Nor would both be lords (*īśvara*), which would constitute a contradiction.
However, there is no fault [in our position], because under the sovereignty of that one [Lord], all those who conform to His intention attain unanimity.

In this regard, since those who have acquired their power through causes and whose births are dependent on those causes are unequal—being perceived as possessing specific distinctions—that very one who possesses eternal sovereignty is their supreme ruler; thus, the wise are dependent upon Him and do not exercise independent control over the Supreme Lord’s activity of creation and dissolution. //17//
